title: Latency tessellation scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
- Quick personal notebook exploring a lightweight priming strategy I called tessellation: split incoming long context traffic into staggered tiles to opportunistically warm KV cache and local attention kernels while keeping per-request extra tokens low. Aim: reduce p99 tail for mixed short+long request mixes with constrained batch windows.

Background / Motivation:
- Observed recurring high p99 during mixed workloads where occasional long-context requests cause cache churn and block small short requests for multiple batches.
- We already have prefix caching and continuous batching, but coldness propagation still spikes tails when sequences collide on same GPU.
- Tessellation idea: when a long request arrives, rather than fully prime with the whole context up-front, split priming into small tiles that are dispatched early, overlapping with other work so that large KV state is gradually populated without monopolizing batch slots.

Hypothesis:
- For 95-99.9% traffic, staggered small priming tiles reduce blocking on long requests and amortize warmup cost across many small requests, improving short-request latency at little cost to throughput.

Experiment config (runs):
- HW: g4dn.12xlarge emulation node (4 x A100 simulated profile), single model shard.
- Model: redwood-open-7b_v1, fp16, 2-stage kv cache.
- Baseline mode: full-prefix-prime then generate (current prod config).
- Tessellation mode: tile_size=128 tokens, max_tiles=8, inter-tile-gap=20ms, eager-first-tile=true.
- Arrival mix: 85% short requests (len 32), 15% long requests (len 2048). Poisson arrival with bursts (lambda varying to reach 250 qps sustained).
- Batch timeout: 8ms, max batch size 64.
- Measurement window: 30 minutes steady-state after 10 minute warmup.

Key metrics collected:
- p50, p95, p99 latencies for short and long requests
- throughput (tokens/s), successful qps
- kv-cache hit rate per shard across time
- CPU/GPU utilization and queue depth

Raw run summaries (median of 3 runs):
- Baseline:
  - short p50: 18 ms, p95: 42 ms, p99: 138 ms
  - long p50: 420 ms, p95: 1100 ms, p99: 2100 ms
  - tokens/s: 180k, qps: 240
  - kv hit rate: initial ramp 22% -> steady 64%

- Tessellation (tile_size=128, gap=20ms):
  - short p50: 19 ms, p95: 36 ms, p99: 92 ms  <-- big win for short tail
  - long p50: 480 ms, p95: 1250 ms, p99: 2200 ms   <-- slight long tail regression
  - tokens/s: 168k (-7%), qps: 233
  - kv hit rate: ramp faster 35% -> steady 71%

- Tessellation aggressive (tile_size=256, gap=10ms, max_tiles=12):
  - short p50: 20 ms, p95: 40 ms, p99: 110 ms
  - long p50: 460 ms, p95: 1200 ms, p99: 2100 ms
  - tokens/s: 172k (-4%), qps: 235
  - kv hit rate: 38% -> 75%

Observations / quick takeaways:
- Tessellation reduced short-request p99 by ~33-40% in the nominal config, with modest overall throughput loss (4-7%). This is promising for latency-sensitive small requests.
- Long-request tails are slightly worse in some configs, likely because interleaving priming prevents contiguous fast prefix execution that would otherwise make the long request faster.
- Kv-cache ramp is faster with tessellation, which suggests more even distribution of priming across shards and reduced hot-blocking.
- Aggressive tiling increases cache warmup but starts to eat throughput; need careful knob tuning per SLA class.

Unresolved questions / confounders:
- Our simulated HW may understate PCIe/host transfer overheads for many small tiles; need a run on dedicated-gpu fleet to confirm.
- Inter-tile gap of 20ms was heuristic; could adaptively choose gap based on queue depth.
- Impact with model variants (quantized 4bit) unknown; quantized kernels have different priming cost curve.
- Interaction with autoscaling cooldowns and eviction policies untested.

Quick experiments to run next (priority order):
1) Small run on dedicated cluster (dedicated pool) with real A100 to measure host transfer overheads (tag: infra-verify).
2) Add adaptive-gap policy: gap = min(20ms, 0.5 * batch_timeout) and compare.
3) Per-tenant rollout sim: run with mixed priorities to ensure no unintended starvation of long requests for enterprise customers.
4) Try tile-first-eager=false to see if delaying first tile changes tail behaviour.
5) Evaluate with quantized 4-bit variant and measure kernel-level priming costs.

Notes to self / heuristics learned:
- Tune tile_size to be aligned with attention window cut points (128/256) to avoid partial-kernel penalties.
- If gap < kernel startup time, tiles coalesce anyway — wasted split. Need instrumentation that reports whether tiles merged in runtime.
- Track per-request priming overhead vs generation time; if priming is >30% of gen time, tessellation unlikely to help.

Slack breadcrumbs and next sync:
- Pushed initial sketch to Confluence for context: Confluence link above.
- Dropped a prototype branch for the router / scheduler: PR link above (WIP).
- Ping Asha for infra slot on dedicated pool, Noah for telemetry traces.

- [ ] Draft short write-up for eng-serving-runtime weekly sync

Microsummary (1 sentence):
- Tessellation looks promising as a low-friction strategy to pull down short-request tails by staggering priming work, but needs careful tuning to avoid regressing long-request SLAs and to validate on real HW.
